cities.name: Jaipur
cities.overview: The Pink City and Rajasthan's capital: a planned old town of bazaars and palaces, ringed by the hill forts of the Aravallis.
cities.history: Founded in 1727 by Sawai Jai Singh II, who moved the Kachwaha capital down from Amer to a new walled city laid out on a grid. The old town was painted pink for the visit of the Prince of Wales in 1876, and the colour stayed.

cities.name: Udaipur
cities.overview: The city of lakes, built around Lake Pichola with the palace of the Mewar kings along its eastern shore.
cities.history: Founded by Maharana Udai Singh II in the 16th century as the new capital of Mewar, after Chittor became too exposed to attack. It remained the seat of the Sisodia rulers until Independence.

cities.name: Jodhpur
cities.overview: The Blue City on the edge of the Thar, its old quarter of indigo houses spread below the cliff of Mehrangarh.
cities.history: Founded in 1459 by Rao Jodha of the Rathore clan as the capital of Marwar. It grew rich on the desert trade routes and stayed a princely state until 1949.

cities.name: Jaisalmer
cities.overview: The 'Golden City' rises out of the Thar Desert, built almost entirely from yellow sandstone. It is the base for camel safaris and nights under the stars in the dunes.
cities.history: Founded in 1156 by Rawal Jaisal of the Bhati clan. The golden sandstone town prospered as a stop on the camel caravan routes to Central Asia, and its fort is still lived in today.

cities.name: Abhaneri
cities.overview: A small village in Dausa district, about 95 km from Jaipur, known for one of India's deepest and most striking stepwells.

cities.name: Ranakpur
cities.overview: A village in a forested valley of the Aravallis in Pali district, between Udaipur and Jodhpur, known for its marble Jain temple.

cities.name: Bikaner
cities.overview: A desert city of red sandstone in the northern Thar, known for its fort, its camels and the rat temple at Deshnoke.
cities.history: Founded in 1488 by Rao Bika, a son of Rao Jodha of Jodhpur. It became one of the wealthiest states of the Thar, and Maharaja Ganga Singh brought it a canal and a railway in the 20th century.

cities.name: Ajmer
cities.overview: A hill-ringed city in the middle of Rajasthan and one of India's great Sufi pilgrimage centres, 10 km from Pushkar.

cities.name: Pushkar
cities.overview: A small temple town around a sacred lake, with ghats on every side and a famous camel fair each November.

cities.name: Mount Abu
cities.overview: Rajasthan's only hill station, a green rocky plateau in the Aravallis near the Gujarat border.

cities.name: Chittorgarh
cities.overview: A city on the Berach River, overlooked by the largest fort in Rajasthan and the old capital of Mewar.

cities.name: Kumbhalgarh
cities.overview: A fortress village deep in the Aravallis, between Udaipur and Ranakpur.

cities.name: Nathdwara
cities.overview: A pilgrim town in the Aravallis north of Udaipur, built around the shrine of Shrinathji.

cities.name: Sawai Madhopur
cities.overview: The railway town at the gates of Ranthambore, the best known tiger reserve in north India.

cities.name: Bharatpur
cities.overview: A town on the eastern edge of Rajasthan, known worldwide for the wetland bird sanctuary at its door.

cities.name: Alwar
cities.overview: A city between Delhi and Jaipur, the base for Sariska Tiger Reserve and the ruins of Bhangarh.

cities.name: Bundi
cities.overview: A quiet town in the Hadoti region with a hilltop fort, stepwells and blue lanes that see few tour buses.

cities.name: Neemrana
cities.overview: An old town on the Delhi to Jaipur highway, a popular weekend escape from the capital.

places.name: Amber Fort
places.shortDescription: A honey-coloured hill fort above Maota Lake, famous for its mirror-work Sheesh Mahal and Rajput–Mughal architecture.
places.description: Amber (Amer) Fort climbs a ridge 11 km north of Jaipur, its sandstone and marble halls set around a series of courtyards. Visitors walk or take a jeep up from Maota Lake, pass through the painted Ganesh Pol gateway, and explore the hall of public audience, the private chambers and the Sheesh Mahal, whose ceilings are inlaid with thousands of tiny mirrors. A light and sound show is held in the evenings.
places.history: Raja Man Singh I began the present fort in 1592 on the site of an earlier stronghold, and later rulers of the Kachwaha dynasty expanded it until the capital moved to Jaipur in 1727. It is one of the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013.
places.bestTimeNote: October to March. Arrive at opening time to avoid crowds and heat.

entryFee.note: Composite tickets for several Jaipur monuments are available. Verify current rates on the official site.

timings.hours: 8:00 AM – 5:30 PM; separate evening visit and light show

places.name: Hawa Mahal
places.shortDescription: Jaipur's 'Palace of Winds', a five-storey pink sandstone screen with 953 small windows.
places.description: Hawa Mahal's honeycomb façade is the symbol of Jaipur. Its many latticed windows (jharokhas) let cool air through and allowed royal women to watch street processions without being seen. The building is only one room deep in places; climb to the upper floors for views over the old city and Jantar Mantar. The façade is best photographed from the cafés across the road in the early morning light.
places.history: Built in 1799 by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh and designed by Lal Chand Ustad, the palace is shaped to resemble the crown of Lord Krishna.

entryFee.note: Included in Jaipur's composite ticket. Verify current rates on the official site.

location.address: Hawa Mahal Rd, Badi Choupad, Jaipur, Rajasthan 302002

highlights: Rooftop views of the Pink City

places.name: City Palace, Udaipur
places.shortDescription: Rajasthan's largest palace complex, rising above Lake Pichola with courtyards, museums and lake views.
places.description: The City Palace is a series of palaces built over nearly four centuries, stretching along the eastern shore of Lake Pichola. Its museum takes you through mirror rooms, peacock mosaics, painted walls and royal collections, and the terraces look out to the Lake Palace and Jag Mandir. Boat rides on Lake Pichola leave from the palace jetty.
places.history: Maharana Udai Singh II founded Udaipur and began the palace in 1559 after moving the Mewar capital from Chittorgarh. Later Maharanas added to it, and part of the complex is still home to the former royal family.
places.bestTimeNote: September to March; the lakes are fullest after the monsoon.

entryFee.note: Ticketed; prices differ for the museum, camera and boat ride. Check the official site.

location.address: City Palace Complex, Old City, Udaipur, Rajasthan 313001

places.name: Mehrangarh Fort
places.shortDescription: A massive fort on a 120-metre cliff above Jodhpur's blue old city, with one of Rajasthan's best museums.
places.description: Mehrangarh towers over Jodhpur with walls up to 36 metres high. Inside, carved palaces such as Moti Mahal and Phool Mahal hold a museum of palanquins, howdahs, weapons, paintings and textiles; the audio guide is excellent. The ramparts give sweeping views of the blue houses below, and adventurous visitors can ride the zip lines around the fort.
places.history: Rao Jodha, founder of Jodhpur, laid the foundation in 1459. The fort was expanded by later Rathore rulers and has never been taken by siege.

entryFee.note: Includes the museum. Verify current rates on the official site.

highlights: Rampart views of the Blue City

places.name: Jaisalmer Fort
places.shortDescription: A 'living fort' of golden sandstone where about a quarter of the old city's people still live.
places.description: Known as Sonar Qila (the Golden Fort), Jaisalmer Fort glows yellow in the afternoon sun. Inside its walls are narrow lanes of houses, shops, guesthouses, a royal palace museum and a group of finely carved Jain temples. It is one of the few forts in the world still lived in, which also makes it fragile: water use from tourism has damaged its foundations.
places.history: Rawal Jaisal founded the fort in 1156 on Trikuta hill. It sat on a key caravan route, and its merchants grew rich on the trade, building the carved havelis seen in the town below. It is one of the six Hill Forts of Rajasthan on the UNESCO World Heritage list.
places.bestTimeNote: November to February; desert summers are extremely hot.

entryFee.note: Free to enter the fort. The palace museum and Jain temples charge separately.

timings.hours: Fort open all day; palace museum about 9:00 AM – 6:00 PM

places.name: Sam Sand Dunes
places.shortDescription: Rolling Thar Desert dunes 40 km from Jaisalmer, known for camel rides, jeep safaris and desert camps.
places.description: Sam is the most popular place to see the Thar Desert's dunes. Visitors arrive in the late afternoon for camel or jeep rides across the sand, watch the sunset, and stay the night in tented camps with Rajasthani folk music and dance. For quieter dunes, travellers head to Khuri, south of Jaisalmer.
places.bestTimeNote: November to February. The Desert Festival is held in February.

timings.hours: Open all day; sunset is the busiest time

places.name: Chand Baori
places.shortDescription: A 9th-century stepwell with about 3,500 steps arranged in perfect symmetry down thirteen storeys.
places.description: Chand Baori is a square stepwell whose zig-zag flights of steps drop about 20 metres to a pool of water. It was built to collect and store rainwater in this dry region, and the deep shaft stays noticeably cooler than the surface. Across the road is the ruined but finely carved Harshat Mata Temple. The site is an easy detour on the Jaipur–Agra highway.
places.history: The stepwell is believed to have been built by King Chanda of the Nikumbha dynasty in the 8th–9th century. Pavilions on its upper side were added later in the Mughal period.
highlights: Easy stop between Jaipur and Agra

places.name: Ranakpur Jain Temple
places.shortDescription: A white marble Jain temple with over 1,400 intricately carved pillars, no two alike.
places.description: The Chaturmukha Dharana Vihara at Ranakpur is dedicated to Adinath, the first Jain tirthankara. Light falls through its domes onto a forest of carved pillars and ceilings, and the temple has four entrances facing the four directions. Visitors must dress modestly and leave leather items outside; an audio guide is available.
places.history: Built in the 15th century by the merchant Dharna Shah with the support of Rana Kumbha of Mewar, to a design by the architect Depa.

entryFee.note: Free for Indian visitors; foreign visitors and cameras are charged. Check at the temple.

location.address: Ranakpur, Desuri tehsil, Pali district, Rajasthan 306702

places.name: City Palace, Jaipur
places.shortDescription: The royal seat of Jaipur at the heart of the old city, with courtyards, gateways and a working royal residence.
places.description: A complex of courtyards, gardens and halls in the middle of the walled city, part of it still home to the former royal family. The rest is a museum of textiles, arms and the enormous silver urns that carried Ganges water to London.
places.history: Construction began soon after Jaipur was founded by Sawai Jai Singh II in 1727, and later rulers kept adding to it.
highlights: Pritam Niwas Chowk and its four seasonal gates

places.name: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur
places.shortDescription: Nineteen giant astronomical instruments in stone, including the world's largest stone sundial. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.description: An open-air observatory of masonry instruments that measure time, track stars and predict eclipses. It still works, and the guides will read the time off the great sundial to within seconds.
places.history: Completed in 1734 by Sawai Jai Singh II, a king who was also a serious astronomer. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

places.name: Nahargarh Fort
places.shortDescription: A hill fort on the Aravalli edge above Jaipur, the city's favourite sunset point.
places.description: Nahargarh sits on the ridge directly above the old city, and its terraces give the widest view of Jaipur spread out below. Inside is Madhavendra Bhawan, a palace of linked suites built for the queens.
places.history: Together with Amber and Jaigarh, it formed a defensive ring around the city.
highlights: Road along the ridge to Jaigarh

places.name: Jaigarh Fort
places.shortDescription: The military fort above Amer, on Cheel ka Teela, home to one of the largest cannons on wheels.
places.description: A rugged military stronghold on the hill directly above Amber Fort and Maota Lake, linked to it by a tunnel. It has water tanks, armouries and the huge Jaivana cannon.
places.history: It was built to protect Amer and its palace, and it served as the Kachwahas' cannon foundry.

places.name: Jal Mahal
places.shortDescription: A palace that seems to float in the middle of Man Sagar Lake, on the road from Jaipur to Amer.
places.description: A low sandstone palace standing in the waters of Man Sagar Lake, seen best from the promenade on the road to Amer. Visitors cannot go inside, but it is one of the most photographed views in the city.
highlights: Winter migratory birds on the lake

places.name: Albert Hall Museum
places.shortDescription: Rajasthan's oldest museum, an Indo-Saracenic landmark in Ram Niwas Garden, lit up every evening.
places.description: The state museum of Rajasthan holds miniature paintings, carpets, armour, sculpture and an Egyptian mummy. The building itself is as much of a draw as the collection.
places.history: A fine example of Indo-Saracenic architecture, standing outside the city wall opposite New Gate.

places.name: Galtaji
places.shortDescription: The monkey temple: a chain of temples and sacred tanks in a narrow gorge, 10 km east of Jaipur.
places.description: An ancient pilgrimage site built into a crevice in the hills, with temples and natural spring-fed tanks stepping up the gorge. Large troops of macaques live here, and they rule the place.

places.name: Lake Pichola
places.shortDescription: The lake Udaipur was built around, an artificial lake from 1362 with palaces on its islands.
places.description: A boat ride on Pichola gives the classic view of Udaipur: the long City Palace on one shore, the white Lake Palace and Jag Mandir on the water, and ghats full of washing and prayer.
places.history: Created in 1362 and named after the nearby village of Picholi.
highlights: View of the City Palace from the water

places.name: Jag Mandir
places.shortDescription: An island palace on Lake Pichola, also called the Lake Garden Palace, reached by boat.
places.description: A palace of marble and courtyards on an island in the south of the lake, reached by boat from the City Palace jetty. Stone elephants guard the water gate.
places.history: Its construction is credited to three Maharanas of Mewar in the 17th century.
highlights: Stone elephants at the water gate
Boat ride from the City Palace

images.credit: No machine-readable author provided. Philbrest assumed (based on copyright claims)

places.name: Fateh Sagar Lake
places.shortDescription: Udaipur's second lake, north of Pichola, with a lively promenade and a garden island.
places.description: A broad lake with hills around it and a long road along the bank that fills with locals in the evening. Boats go to Nehru Park on an island in the middle.
places.history: An artificial lake named after Maharana Fateh Singh of Mewar.
highlights: Evening promenade at Moti Magri road

places.name: Saheliyon-ki-Bari
places.shortDescription: The Garden of the Maidens: fountains, kiosks, a lotus pool and marble elephants in north Udaipur.
places.description: A shaded formal garden built for the royal women, known for its fountains that run on water pressure alone. It is a calm hour away from the old city.

places.name: Jagdish Temple
places.shortDescription: A large temple just outside the City Palace, in continuous worship since 1651.
places.description: A carved Indo-Aryan temple dedicated to Vishnu, reached by a steep flight of steps from the old city's main crossing. The aarti draws locals every evening.
places.history: In continuous worship since 1651.

places.name: Monsoon Palace
places.shortDescription: Sajjangarh, a hilltop palace above Fateh Sagar with Udaipur's best sunset views.
places.description: A white palace on a peak in the Aravallis west of the city, surrounded by a wildlife sanctuary. Few come for the rooms; nearly everyone comes for the sunset across the lakes.
places.history: Named Sajjangarh after Maharana Sajjan Singh of Mewar, who commissioned it.

places.name: Umaid Bhawan Palace
places.shortDescription: One of the world's largest private residences, part royal home, part Taj hotel, part museum.
places.description: A golden-sandstone Art Deco palace on Chittar Hill, split between the former royal family, a luxury hotel and a small museum of clocks and vintage cars that is open to everyone.
places.history: Named after Maharaja Umaid Singh, grandfather of the present owner.

places.name: Jaswant Thada
places.shortDescription: A white marble memorial near Mehrangarh, sometimes called the Taj Mahal of Marwar.
places.description: A serene cenotaph of carved marble beside a small lake, with the fort on the cliff behind it. Thin marble panels glow in the sun.
places.history: Built by Maharaja Sardar Singh in 1899 in memory of his father, Maharaja Jaswant Singh II.

places.name: Mandore
places.shortDescription: The old capital of Marwar 9 km north of Jodhpur, with royal cenotaphs in a walled garden.
places.description: Temple-like memorials to the Rathore rulers stand in red sandstone among gardens and old ruins. Langurs roam the grounds, and the place is popular with local families.
places.history: Mandore was the seat of power in Marwar before Rao Jodha founded Jodhpur.

places.name: Gadisar Lake
places.shortDescription: The old water supply of Jaisalmer, a rainwater lake with chhatris and a carved gateway.
places.description: Small shrines stand out in the water, and the lake is reached through the carved Tilon-ki-Pol gate. It is at its best at sunrise, with the fort glowing to the north.
places.history: Built by the city's founder Rawal Jaisal in 1156 and rebuilt by Rawal Gadsi around 1367.

places.name: Kuldhara
places.shortDescription: An abandoned Paliwal Brahmin village in the desert west of Jaisalmer, empty for two centuries.
places.description: Rows of roofless stone houses stand silent in the scrub. No one is certain why the people left, and local legend calls it a cursed village.
places.history: Established around the 13th century and abandoned by the early 19th century, for reasons that are still unclear.
highlights: Stop on the road to Sam dunes

places.name: Junagarh Fort
places.shortDescription: An undefeated fort in the flat centre of Bikaner, with lavishly painted palace rooms.
places.description: Unusually, this fort is on level ground and not on a hill. Inside, one palace leads to another, with gold leaf, mirror work and a biplane from the First World War.
places.history: Originally called Chintamani, it was renamed Junagarh, or Old Fort, in the early 20th century when the family moved to Lalgarh Palace.

places.name: Karni Mata Temple
places.shortDescription: The rat temple of Deshnoke, 30 km from Bikaner, where thousands of sacred rats are fed and protected.
places.description: Thousands of black rats live in this marble temple, and they are revered as the kin of the goddess Karni Mata. You walk in barefoot, and seeing a rare white rat is thought to be good luck.

places.name: Ajmer Sharif Dargah
places.shortDescription: The shrine of the Sufi saint Moinuddin Chishti, one of the most visited Muslim shrines in India.
places.description: People of all faiths come here to tie threads and offer flowers at the saint's tomb. Qawwali singers fill the courtyards in the evening, and the annual Urs draws huge crowds.
places.history: A complex of tombs and a mosque that grew around the grave of Mu'in al-Din Chishti, founder of the Chishti order in India.

sources.title: Shrine of Mu'in al-Din Chishti – Wikipedia

places.name: Ana Sagar Lake
places.shortDescription: A 12th-century artificial lake in Ajmer, with marble pavilions along the bank.
places.description: Mughal pavilions in white marble line the embankment at Daulat Bagh, and the lake is a quiet evening spot for the city.
places.history: Built by Arnoraja, the grandfather of Prithviraj Chauhan, between 1135 and 1150.

places.name: Pushkar Lake
places.shortDescription: A sacred lake for Hindus, ringed by 52 bathing ghats and hundreds of temples.
places.description: Pilgrims bathe at the ghats at dawn and dusk, and the sound of bells and chanting carries across the water. Hindu scriptures call it Tirtha Raj, the king of pilgrimage places.
places.bestTimeNote: The Pushkar Camel Fair falls around the full moon of Kartik, usually in November.

images.credit: Felipe Skroski from Wellington, New Zealand

places.name: Brahma Temple, Pushkar
places.shortDescription: One of very few temples in the world dedicated to Brahma, close to the sacred lake.
places.description: A modest temple with a red spire and a marble floor set with coins left by pilgrims. Its rarity is what draws them: Brahma is seldom worshipped on his own.

places.name: Dilwara Temples
places.shortDescription: Jain temples near Mount Abu, whose white marble carving is among the finest in India.
places.description: Plain outside and astonishing inside: the ceilings and pillars are carved with marble lace so fine it seems unreal. They remain active places of worship, and photography is not allowed.
places.history: A group of Svetambara Jain temples and one of the five great Jain pilgrimage sites.

places.name: Nakki Lake
places.shortDescription: The lake at the centre of Mount Abu, with boating and odd rock shapes along the bank.
places.description: A small green lake surrounded by hills and the town's market. Paddle boats are the main activity, and the Toad Rock is a short climb away.

places.name: Kumbhalgarh Fort
places.shortDescription: The Great Wall of India: a Mewar fortress with one of the world's longest continuous walls.
places.description: A massive fort on the western Aravallis, its wall running for kilometres over ridges and valleys. Inside are hundreds of temples and a palace at the top with a view over the Marwar plains.
places.history: A UNESCO World Heritage Site as one of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan, and the birthplace of Maharana Pratap.

places.name: Chittorgarh Fort
places.shortDescription: One of India's largest forts and the old capital of Mewar, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.description: A whole ruined city on a hill above the plains, with palaces, temples, reservoirs and the two great towers. Few places in India carry as much Rajput legend.
places.history: Sacked three times, and remembered for the mass self-immolations of its women. Mewar's capital moved to Udaipur after the third siege in 1568.
highlights: Vijay Stambha, the Tower of Victory

places.name: Ranthambore National Park
places.shortDescription: North India's best known tiger reserve, where tigers are often seen in daylight among old ruins.
places.description: Dry forest, lakes and rocky hills, with ruined pavilions and a fort for a backdrop. The tigers here are famously easy to see, and leopards, sloth bears and crocodiles live here too.
places.history: Once the hunting ground of the Maharajas of Jaipur.
places.bestTimeNote: Core zones close in the monsoon, roughly July to September.
highlights: Tiger safaris by jeep and canter

places.name: Ranthambore Fort
places.shortDescription: A hill fort inside the tiger reserve, with temples and tanks, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places.description: The fort stands on a rock high above the forest. You pass through a series of gates to reach the old palaces and the Ganesh temple, which draws pilgrims every day.
places.history: One of the Hill Forts of Rajasthan on the UNESCO list.

places.name: Keoladeo National Park
places.shortDescription: A UNESCO wetland at Bharatpur, home to thousands of resident and migratory birds each winter.
places.description: A flat mosaic of marsh and woodland best explored by bicycle or cycle rickshaw. Each winter, the wetlands fill with ducks, geese, cranes and raptors, as well as the resident storks and herons.
places.history: A former royal duck-hunting reserve, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
highlights: Cycle rickshaw with a trained guide

places.name: Sariska Tiger Reserve
places.shortDescription: A reserve of dry forest and grassland in the Aravallis, in Alwar district, with reintroduced tigers.
places.description: Scrub forest and rocky valleys, with safari drives past old temples and the ruined Kankwari Fort. Sambar, nilgai and langurs are common, and the tigers were brought back after being lost here in the 2000s.

places.name: Bhangarh Fort
places.shortDescription: A well-preserved 16th-century ruined town, famous as one of India's most haunted places.
places.description: Bazaars, temples and a palace stand roofless below the Aravalli hills. The Archaeological Survey of India bars entry after dark, and that has helped the ghost stories along.
places.history: Established during the rule of Bhagwant Das as the residence of his second son, Madho Singh.

places.name: Taragarh Fort, Bundi
places.shortDescription: A hill fort above Bundi with ruined ramparts, reservoirs and monkeys for company.
places.description: An overgrown fort on a steep hill above the town, reached by a stiff walk from the palace. Just below it, the Bundi Palace holds some of Rajasthan's finest wall paintings.

places.name: Shrinathji Temple
places.shortDescription: A major Krishna shrine at Nathdwara, centre of the Pushtimarg tradition, about 50 km from Udaipur.
places.description: Worship here treats the deity as a living child, with the image dressed, fed and put to bed through the day. Darshan opens only at set times, and crowds surge in when it does.
places.history: Shrinathji is the central deity of the Pushtimarg sect established by Vallabhacharya.

places.name: Neemrana Fort
places.shortDescription: A 15th-century hillside fort-palace on the Delhi to Jaipur road, now a heritage hotel.
places.description: A fort stepping down a hillside in terraces, restored as a heritage hotel and popular for weekend trips from Delhi. There's also a zipline over the walls.
